clinicalPearls: Thin-walled cysts lying within the broad ligament or mesosalpinx, between the fallopian tube and the ovary, and separate from ovarian tissue
They arise from embryological remnants, either mesonephric (Wolffian) or paramesonephric (Müllerian) in origin
The hydatid of Morgagni is a small pedunculated paramesonephric remnant that hangs near the fimbrial end of the tube
Most are asymptomatic and found incidentally at imaging or surgery, appearing as simple unilocular cysts
On ultrasound, demonstrating that the cyst is separate from a normal ipsilateral ovary is the key to diagnosis
Larger cysts may cause pressure symptoms or undergo torsion, sometimes taking the adjacent tube or ovary with them
Management ranges from expectant observation for small simple cysts to surgical excision for symptomatic, enlarging, or atypical lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Paratubal cysts develop from vestigial embryological structures in the broad ligament. Remnants of the mesonephric duct system, or of the paramesonephric duct that gives rise to the tube, persist and accumulate clear serous fluid to form a cyst. Because they lie alongside but outside the ovary, they retain a simple thin-walled structure; the pedunculated hydatid of Morgagni represents a paramesonephric remnant at the fimbrial end and is prone to torsion on its narrow stalk.
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrating a cyst separate from a normal ovary
Application of the split sign to confirm the ovary is distinct from the cyst
Magnetic resonance imaging to localise larger or complex cysts
Tumour markers where features are atypical
Surgical and histological assessment when excision is undertaken
redFlags: Torsion involving the cyst, tube, or ovary presenting with acute pain
Rapid growth or solid vascular components suggesting a rare neoplastic change in the wall
A large cyst causing significant pressure symptoms
Features that cannot confidently be distinguished from ovarian malignancy
reference.prognosis: Paratubal cysts are benign with an excellent outlook; simple cysts require little or no intervention, and surgical removal is curative when symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty warrant it.
pitfalls: Mistaking a paratubal cyst for an ovarian cyst and misdirecting management
Failing to recognise torsion involving the adjacent tube or ovary
Overlooking the rare borderline or neoplastic change that can arise in the cyst wall
Unnecessary intervention for small, asymptomatic, clearly benign cysts
management: Manage small, asymptomatic, simple cysts expectantly, as they are benign and usually found incidentally
Confirm on transvaginal ultrasound that the cyst is separate from a normal ipsilateral ovary, using the split sign, before deciding on management
Offer surgical excision by laparoscopic cystectomy for cysts that are large, symptomatic, enlarging or diagnostically uncertain
Treat adnexal torsion as a surgical emergency with prompt laparoscopy, detorsion and cyst removal, preserving the tube and ovary where viable
Send excised tissue for histological confirmation of the benign diagnosis
Use MRI or tumour markers when imaging features are atypical to exclude a neoplastic lesion
